title: Book 21 — The trial of the axes, during which Odysseus reveals himself to Eumaeus and Philoetius
paragraphs: Athena now put it into Penelope’s mind to make the suitors test their skill with the bow and iron axes in a contest among themselves, as a way to bring about their destruction. She went upstairs and got the storeroom key, which was made of bronze with an ivory handle. Then she went with her maids to the storeroom at the end of the house, where her husband’s treasures of gold, bronze, and wrought iron were kept, and where his bow was also stored, along with the quiver full of deadly arrows that had been given to him by a friend he had met in Lacedaemon—Iphitus, son of Eurytus. The two had encountered each other in Messene at the house of Ortilochus, where Odysseus was staying to recover a debt owed by the whole people. The Messenians had stolen three hundred sheep from Ithaca and sailed away with them and their shepherds. To recover these sheep, Odysseus had taken a long journey while still quite young, sent on this mission by his father and the other chiefs. Iphitus had also gone there to try to get back twelve brood mares he had lost, along with their mule foals. These mares would be his death in the end, for when he went to the house of Zeus’s son, mighty Heracles, who performed such incredible feats of valor, Heracles shamefully killed him, though Iphitus was his guest, for Heracles neither feared heaven’s vengeance nor respected his own table that he had set before Iphitus, but killed him despite everything and kept the mares for himself. It was while claiming these mares that Iphitus met Odysseus and gave him the bow that mighty Eurytus had carried, which had been left to his son when he died. Odysseus gave him in return a sword and spear, and this was the beginning of a strong friendship, though they never visited each other’s homes, for Zeus’s son Heracles killed Iphitus before they could do so. This bow, given to him by Iphitus, had not been taken by Odysseus when he sailed for Troy. He had used it as long as he lived at home, but had left it behind as a keepsake from a valued friend.

Penelope soon reached the oak threshold of the storeroom. The carpenter had planed it smooth and drawn a line on it to make it perfectly straight, then set the door posts into it and hung the doors. She loosened the strap from the door handle, put in the key, and drove it straight home to shoot back the bolts that held the doors. These flew open with a noise like a bull bellowing in a meadow, and Penelope stepped onto the raised platform where chests stood containing fine linen and clothes laid away with fragrant herbs. Reaching up from there, she took down the bow with its case from the peg where it hung. She sat down with it across her knees, weeping bitterly as she took the bow from its case. When her tears had given her relief, she went to the gallery where the suitors were, carrying the bow and quiver with its many deadly arrows. Her maids came with her, bearing a chest containing much iron and bronze that her husband had won as prizes. When she reached the suitors, she stood by one of the pillars supporting the roof of the gallery, holding a veil before her face, with a maid on either side of her. Then she spoke:

“Listen to me, you suitors who persist in abusing the hospitality of this house because its owner has been long absent, with no other excuse than that you want to marry me. Since this is the prize you’re competing for, I will bring out the mighty bow of Odysseus. Whoever among you can string it most easily and send his arrow through each of the twelve axes—him will I follow, leaving this house of my lawful husband, so beautiful and rich in wealth. Even so, I’m sure I will remember it in my dreams.”

As she spoke, she told Eumaeus to set the bow and pieces of iron before the suitors. Eumaeus wept as he took them to do as she commanded. Nearby, the stockman also wept when he saw his master’s bow, but Antinous scolded them. “You country fools,” he said, “silly simpletons! Why should you add to your mistress’s sorrows by crying like this? She has enough to grieve her in losing her husband. Sit still and eat your dinner in silence, or go outside if you want to cry, and leave the bow behind. We suitors will have to compete for it with all our might, for we’ll find it no easy matter to string such a bow as this. There isn’t a man among us who is another Odysseus. I have seen him and remember him, though I was only a child then.”

This is what he said, but all the time he expected to be able to string the bow and shoot through the iron. In fact, he would be the first to taste arrows from the hands of Odysseus, whom he was dishonoring in his own house—and encouraging the others to do the same.

Then Telemachus spoke. “Great heavens!” he exclaimed. “Zeus must have robbed me of my senses. Here is my dear and excellent mother saying she will leave this house and marry again, yet I’m laughing and enjoying myself as though nothing were happening. But suitors, since the contest has been agreed upon, let it proceed. It’s for a woman whose equal cannot be found in Pylos, Argos, Mycenae, or even in Ithaca or on the mainland. You know this as well as I do—what need do I have to praise my mother? Come then, make no excuses for delay, but let’s see whether you can string the bow or not. I too will try it, for if I can string it and shoot through the iron, I won’t let my mother leave this house with a stranger, not if I can win the same prizes my father won before me.”

As he spoke, he sprang from his seat, threw off his crimson cloak, and took his sword from his shoulder. First he set up the axes in a row, in a long trench he had dug for them and made straight with a line. Then he stamped the earth tight around them, and everyone was surprised to see him set them up so precisely, though he had never seen anything like this before. When this was done, he went onto the pavement to try the bow. Three times he tugged at it, trying with all his strength to draw the string, and three times he had to give up, though he hoped to string the bow and shoot through the iron. He was trying for the fourth time and would have strung it, but Odysseus signaled him to stop despite all his eagerness. So he said:

“Alas! I must always be weak and powerless, or I’m too young and haven’t yet reached my full strength to be able to defend myself if anyone attacks me. You others who are stronger than I am, try the bow and settle this contest.”
At this he put the bow down, leaning it against the door that led into the house, with the arrow standing against the top of the bow. Then he sat down on the seat he had left, and Antinous said:
“Come forward, each of you in turn, moving toward the right from where the cupbearer begins when he hands the wine around.”

The rest agreed, and Leiodes, son of Oenops, was the first to rise. He was the suitors’ sacrificial priest and sat in the corner near the mixing-bowl. He was the only man who hated their evil deeds and was disgusted with the others. He was now first to take the bow and arrow, so he went onto the pavement to make his attempt. But he couldn’t string the bow, for his hands were weak and unused to hard work, so they quickly grew tired. He said to the suitors, “My friends, I cannot string it. Let another try. This bow will take the life and soul from many a chief among us, for it’s better to die than to live after missing the prize we’ve striven for so long and which has kept us together so long. Someone among us is even now hoping and praying to marry Penelope, but when he has seen this bow and tried it, let him court and offer wedding gifts to some other woman, and let Penelope marry whoever makes her the best offer and whose fate it is to win her.”
At this he put the bow down, leaning it against the door with the arrow standing against the tip of the bow. Then he returned to his seat, and Antinous rebuked him, saying:

“Leiodes, what are you talking about? Your words are terrible and intolerable—it makes me angry to listen to you. Shall this bow take the life of many chiefs among us merely because you cannot bend it yourself? True, you weren’t born to be an archer, but there are others who will soon string it.”

Then he said to Melanthius the goatherd, “Quick, light a fire in the courtyard and set a seat nearby with a sheepskin on it. Bring us also a large ball of lard from what they have in the house. Let us warm the bow and grease it—we’ll then try it again and bring the contest to an end.”

Melanthius lit the fire and set a seat covered with sheepskins beside it. He also brought a great ball of lard from what they had in the house, and the suitors warmed the bow and tried it again, but none of them was nearly strong enough to string it. Nevertheless, there still remained Antinous and Eurymachus, who were the ringleaders among the suitors and by far the foremost among them all.
Then the swineherd and the stockman left the gallery together, and Odysseus followed them. When they had gotten outside the gates and outer courtyard, Odysseus said to them quietly:

“Stockman, and you, swineherd, I have something on my mind that I’m not sure whether to say or not, but I think I will say it. What kind of men would you be to stand by Odysseus if some god should bring him back here suddenly? Tell me which you would choose—to side with the suitors or with Odysseus?”
“Father Zeus,” answered the stockman, “if only you would make it so! If some god were to bring Odysseus back, you would see with what strength and determination I would fight for him.”

Eumaeus prayed in the same words to all the gods that Odysseus might return. When he saw for certain what their feelings were, Odysseus said, “It is I, Odysseus, who stands here. I have suffered much, but at last, in the twentieth year, I have returned to my own country. I find that you two alone of all my servants are glad that I should return, for I haven’t heard any of the others praying for my homecoming. To you two, therefore, I will reveal the truth as it will be. If heaven delivers the suitors into my hands, I will find wives for both of you, give you houses and land close to my own, and you shall be to me like brothers and friends of Telemachus. I will now give you convincing proof so you may know me and be certain. Look, here is the scar from the boar’s tooth that ripped me when I was hunting on Mount Parnassus with the sons of Autolycus.”

As he spoke, he drew his rags aside from the great scar. When they had examined it thoroughly, they both wept over Odysseus, threw their arms around him, and kissed his head and shoulders, while Odysseus kissed their hands and faces in return. The sun would have set on their mourning if Odysseus hadn’t stopped them and said:

“Stop your weeping, in case someone comes outside and sees us and tells those inside. When you go in, do so separately, not together. I will go first, and you follow afterward. Let this also be our signal; the suitors will all try to prevent me from getting hold of the bow and quiver. Therefore, Eumaeus, when you’re carrying it around, place it in my hands and tell the women to close the doors of their quarters. If they hear any groaning or uproar as of men fighting in the house, they must not come out—they must stay quiet and remain where they are at their work. And I charge you, Philoetius, to secure the doors of the outer courtyard and bind them fast at once.”
Having said this, he went back to the house and took the seat he had left. Soon his two servants followed him inside.

At this moment the bow was in Eurymachus’s hands, who was warming it by the fire, but even so he couldn’t string it, and he was deeply troubled. He heaved a deep sigh and said, “I grieve for myself and for all of us. I’m sorry that I must give up the marriage, but I don’t care nearly as much about that, for there are plenty of other women in Ithaca and elsewhere. What troubles me most is the fact that we’re so much weaker than Odysseus that we cannot string his bow. This will disgrace us in the eyes of future generations.”

“It won’t be so, Eurymachus,” said Antinous, “and you know it yourself. Today is Apollo’s feast throughout all the land—who can string a bow on such a day? Put it aside. As for the axes, they can stay where they are, for no one is likely to come to the house and take them away. Let the cupbearer go around with his cups so we may make our drink offerings and drop this matter of the bow. We’ll tell Melanthius to bring us some goats tomorrow—the best he has. We can then offer thigh bones to Apollo the mighty archer and try the bow again, bringing the contest to an end.”

The rest approved his words, and servants poured water over the guests’ hands, while pages filled the mixing-bowls with wine and water and handed it around after giving every man his drink offering. When they had made their offerings and drunk as much as each desired, Odysseus craftily said:

“Suitors of the illustrious queen, listen so I may speak my mind. I appeal especially to Eurymachus and to Antinous, who has just spoken so reasonably. Stop shooting for now and leave the matter to the gods, but in the morning let heaven give victory to whom it will. For the moment, however, give me the bow so I may test the power of my hands among you all and see whether I still have as much strength as I used to, or whether travel and neglect have ended it.”

This made them all very angry, for they feared he might string the bow. Antinous therefore rebuked him fiercely, saying, “Wretched creature, you don’t have so much as a grain of sense in your whole body. You should think yourself lucky to be allowed to dine unharmed among your betters, without having any smaller portion served to you than we others have had, and to be allowed to hear our conversation. No other beggar or stranger has been allowed to hear what we say among ourselves. The wine must be affecting you badly, as it does with all those who drink too much. It was wine that inflamed the Centaur Eurytion when he was staying with Peirithous among the Lapithae. When the wine got into his head, he went mad and did terrible things in Peirithous’s house. This angered the heroes assembled there, so they rushed at him and cut off his ears and nose, then dragged him through the doorway out of the house. So he went away crazed, bearing the burden of his crime, robbed of understanding. From then on, there was war between mankind and the centaurs, but he brought it on himself through his own drunkenness. In the same way, I can tell you it will go badly for you if you string the bow. You’ll find no mercy from anyone here, for we’ll immediately ship you off to King Echetus, who kills everyone who comes near him. You’ll never escape alive, so drink and keep quiet without picking a fight with men younger than yourself.”

Then Penelope spoke to him. “Antinous,” she said, “it’s not right for you to mistreat any guest of Telemachus who comes to this house. If the stranger should prove strong enough to string the mighty bow of Odysseus, can you suppose he would take me home with him and make me his wife? Even the man himself cannot have such an idea in his mind. None of you need let that disturb your feasting—it would be completely unreasonable.”

“Queen Penelope,” answered Eurymachus, “we don’t suppose this man will take you away with him—that’s impossible. But we’re afraid that some of the common people, men or women among the Achaeans, might go gossiping and say, ‘These suitors are weak men. They’re courting the wife of a brave man whose bow not one of them could string, yet a beggarly tramp who came to the house strung it at once and sent an arrow through the iron.’ This is what will be said, and it will be a scandal against us.”

“Eurymachus,” Penelope answered, “people who persist in devouring the estate of a great chief and dishonoring his house must not expect others to think well of them. Why should you care if men talk as you think they will? This stranger is strong and well-built, and he says he’s of noble birth. Give him the bow and let’s see whether he can string it or not. I say—and it will surely be so—that if Apollo grants him the glory of stringing it, I will give him a cloak and shirt of good quality, with a javelin to keep off dogs and robbers, and a sharp sword. I will also give him sandals and see him sent safely wherever he wants to go.”

Then Telemachus said, “Mother, I am the only man either in Ithaca or in the islands near Elis who has the right to let anyone have the bow or refuse it. No one will force me one way or the other, not even if I choose to give the stranger the bow outright and let him take it away with him. Go then into the house and busy yourself with your daily duties—your loom, your distaff, and managing your servants. This bow is a man’s concern, and mine above all others, for I am master here.”

She went back into the house in wonder, and kept her son’s words in her heart. Then, going upstairs with her handmaids to her room, she mourned her dear husband until Athena sent sweet sleep over her eyelids.

The swineherd now took up the bow and was carrying it to Odysseus, but the suitors shouted at him from all parts of the gallery, and one of them said, “You idiot, where are you taking the bow? Are you out of your mind? If Apollo and the other gods grant our prayer, your own boarhounds will get you into some quiet place and tear you to pieces.”

Eumaeus was frightened by all their shouting, so he put the bow down right there, but Telemachus yelled at him from the other side of the gallery and threatened him, saying, “Father Eumaeus, bring the bow here despite them, or young as I am, I’ll pelt you with stones back to the country, for I’m the better man of the two. I wish I was as much stronger than all the other suitors in the house as I am stronger than you—I would soon send some of them off sick and sorry, for they mean trouble.”

So he spoke, and they all laughed heartily, which put them in a better mood with Telemachus. So Eumaeus brought the bow forward and placed it in Odysseus’s hands. When he had done this, he called Eurycleia aside and said to her, “Eurycleia, Telemachus says you are to close the doors of the women’s quarters. If they hear any groaning or uproar as of men fighting in the house, they must not come out, but must stay quiet and remain where they are at their work.”
Eurycleia did as she was told and closed the doors of the women’s quarters.

Meanwhile, Philoetius slipped quietly out and secured the gates of the outer courtyard. There was a ship’s cable made of papyrus fiber lying in the gatehouse, so he fastened the gates with it and then came back in, resuming the seat he had left and keeping an eye on Odysseus, who now had the bow in his hands and was turning it every way, examining it all over to see whether worms had been eating into its two horns during his absence. Then one would turn to his neighbor saying, “This is some cunning old bow expert. Either he has one like it at home, or he wants to make one, judging by the skillful way the old vagrant handles it.”
Another said, “I hope he’s no more successful in other things than he’s likely to be in stringing this bow.”

But Odysseus, when he had taken it up and examined it thoroughly, strung it as easily as a skilled bard strings a new peg on his lyre and makes the twisted gut fast at both ends. Then he took it in his right hand to test the string, and it sang sweetly under his touch like a swallow’s twitter. The suitors were dismayed and turned pale when they heard it. At that moment, Zeus thundered loudly as a sign, and Odysseus’s heart rejoiced when he heard the omen that the son of crafty Cronus had sent him.

He took an arrow that was lying on the table and laid it on the center grip of the bow, for the rest, which the Achaeans would soon taste, were all inside the quiver. He drew back the notch of the arrow and the string while still seated. When he had taken aim, he let fly, and his arrow pierced every one of the axes’ handle-holes, one after another, until it had gone right through them and into the outer courtyard. Then he said to Telemachus:

“Your guest has not disgraced you, Telemachus. I didn’t miss what I aimed at, and I wasn’t long in stringing my bow. I am still strong, not as the suitors mock me for being. Now, however, it’s time for the Achaeans to prepare supper while there’s still daylight, and then to entertain themselves with song and dance, which are the crowning ornaments of a feast.”
As he spoke, he signaled with his eyebrows, and Telemachus strapped on his sword, grasped his spear, and stood armed beside his father’s seat.
